c.tagline: Franco-German canals, a rose-stone cathedral, and Europe's parliament city.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered with a roof light; ranks sit outside the station and major squares, and Uber and Bolt both operate in the city.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; 17 reaches the police and 15 the medical service (SAMU) directly.

avoid.reason: Outlying housing estates such as Neuhof and Hautepierre offer nothing for visitors and are best skipped after dark; the historic centre is safe.
Pickpockets target crowds around the cathedral, Petite France and especially the Christmas market, and the station area gets sketchy late at night.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed island at the heart of the city, wrapped by the River Ill and crowned by the soaring pink-sandstone cathedral; best for first-timers who want every sight, cafe, and Christmas-market stall within a walkable core.
The postcard quarter of half-timbered houses, flower-lined canals, and covered bridges (Ponts Couverts) on the island's western edge; romantic and photogenic but busy with day-trippers.

A lively student and bohemian district just south-east of the centre, packed with bars, bistros, and the Krutenau market; suits younger travellers and night owls who want to eat and drink where locals do.

The elegant 'German' Neustadt of wide Wilhelmine boulevards, grand civic buildings, and museums laid out during the imperial era and added to the UNESCO site in 2017; calm, stately, and walkable to the centre.
The leafy European quarter around the Parliament and Council of Europe, bordering the Orangerie park and the Robertsau; green, quiet, and diplomatic, a relaxed base away from the crowds.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 4:30 AM to just past midnight, with extended late service on Friday and Saturday nights.
transit.note: Six modern tram lines (A-F), one crossing the Rhine into Kehl, Germany, form the backbone, complemented by an extensive CTS bus network; the compact centre is very walkable and famously bike-friendly with the Velhop bike-share.
transit.pay: Buy single tickets or a 24-hour pass from tram-stop machines, tobacconists, or the CTS app, or tap a contactless bank card on the validators; a single ticket is about EUR 1.90 and a 24-hour Trip pass about EUR 4.60. Validate on boarding.

tip.r: Service is included ('service compris') by law; rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Strasbourg
A soaring Gothic masterpiece in rose-pink sandstone, its 142-metre spire and Renaissance astronomical clock made it the world's tallest building for centuries.
La Petite France
A UNESCO-listed quarter of crooked half-timbered houses, flower-decked canals and old tanners' lanes, the most enchanting corner of Alsace's capital.
Ponts Couverts
Three medieval defensive towers guarding a trio of bridges over the Ill, forming Strasbourg's classic postcard view beside Petite France.
Barrage Vauban
A 17th-century fortified weir by military engineer Vauban, whose rooftop terrace delivers the definitive panorama of the Ponts Couverts and cathedral.
Palais Rohan
An opulent 18th-century episcopal palace housing three museums of fine arts, decorative arts and archaeology behind a majestic riverfront facade.
Maison Kammerzell
Strasbourg's most ornate merchant house, a 1571 confection of carved wooden figures and leaded windows standing beside the cathedral square.
Place Kléber
The city's grand central square, ringed by the pink Aubette palace, famous at Christmas for hosting one of Europe's tallest decorated trees.
European Parliament (Louise Weiss Building)
The striking glass-and-steel seat of European democracy on the Ill's banks, symbolising Strasbourg's role as an official capital of the EU.
Parc de l'Orangerie
Strasbourg's most elegant park, a romantic expanse of lakes, pavilions and free-flying storks facing the European institutions quarter.
Musée Alsacien
A charming museum spread through interconnected Renaissance houses, recreating traditional Alsatian interiors, costumes and folk art around wooden galleried courtyards.

train.note: Strasbourg-Ville is a major TGV hub: high-speed trains reach Paris in about 1h50 and Lyon in ~3h40. Internationally, TGV and DB ICE services run across the Rhine to Karlsruhe, Stuttgart, Frankfurt, and Munich, and SNCF/SBB trains reach Basel and Zurich; the city tram line D even crosses into Kehl, Germany.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches (Flixbus, BlaBlaCar Bus) use the Gare Routiere beside the train station, serving German cities like Frankfurt and Stuttgart plus wider European routes.

ferry.note: Strasbourg is a major Rhine river port for freight and river-cruise ships, but there are no scheduled passenger ferry lines; multi-day Rhine cruises along the Rhine Valley and toward the Black Forest depart seasonally.

full.blurb: An elegant Black Forest spa town of thermal baths, a grand 19th-century casino, and belle-epoque promenades, about 45 min away across the German border.
full.name: Baden-Baden

full.blurb: A sunny university city with a soaring Gothic minster, gateway to the hills, waterfalls, and cuckoo-clock villages of the Black Forest, about 1h10 away.
full.name: Freiburg & the Black Forest

full.blurb: A golden-stone city with a soaring Gothic cathedral and the Centre Pompidou-Metz, about 50 min by TGV.
full.name: Metz

half.blurb: The postcard capital of the Alsace wine road, with 'Little Venice' canals and half-timbered houses, about 30 min by train.
half.name: Colmar

half.blurb: Flower-decked medieval wine villages like Obernai, Riquewihr, and Ribeauville strung along the vineyards south of the city on the Route des Vins.
half.name: Obernai & the Alsace Wine Route

half.blurb: Step across the Rhine into Germany on tram line D to the riverside gardens and shops of Kehl, about 20 minutes from the centre.
half.name: Kehl
